newsitem.title: USA: Wash. state lawmakers angered by stadium ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Wash. state lawmakers angered by stadium ultimatum.

text.p: Lawmakers in the U.S. state of Washington reacted angrily on Tuesday to an ultimatum set by the prospective buyer of the Seattle Seahawks football team, who wants a new stadium built.

Multibillionaire investor Paul Allen, the Microsoft Corp co-founder who last year negotiated an exclusive option to buy the National Football League franchise and keep it in the city, set a deadline of April 3 for legislative approval of a plan to finance construction of a new stadium.
He threatened to back out of the deal if the deadline was not met.
Washington state Representative Steve Van Luven said Allen had no business bossing the legislature around.

"Nobody gives us ultimatums, including Paul Allen," said Van Luven. "I don't care how much money he has. He does not own this place. He does not run this legislature. We run the legislature. We answer to the people."
Stadium-backers such as Van Luven and Democratic Governor Gary Locke vowed to press on. But Van Luven said Allen has made the job harder by irritating lawmakers with his threats to walk away.
Prospects were never bright for passage of the proposal to build a $402 million stadium near downtown Seattle.

The governor's plan to finance the stadium with a package of specialty taxes on sports logo-bearing items, car rentals, admission and parking taxes, and $100 million of Allen's money has failed twice so far in legislative committees.
Whatever package lawmakers can agree on would then go to a statewide vote tentatively scheduled for June 3.
"We still have a chance on this. Until we leave town, this issue is not dead," Van Luven said.
But in a statement issued on Monday night, Allen indicated that three weeks is the most he is willing to wait.

"Since it takes 60 days to provide the required notice for an election, if acceptable legislation is not enacted by April 3 for a June 3 election, I will drop my option to purchase the team," Allen said.
Washington state election officials have echoed the need for quick action. Elections spokesman David Brine said the state and county need about two months to complete preparations for a public vote.
